segments.t: KorTTY recognises when a terminal-based coding agent — KTPH000Claude CodeKTPH001, KTPH002CodexKTPH003, KTPH004Gemini CLIKTPH005, KTPH006MiniMax CodeKTPH007, KTPH008Qwen CodeKTPH009, KTPH010OpenCodeKTPH011, KTPH012Cursor AgentKTPH013, KTPH014AiderKTPH015, KTPH016AmpKTPH017 or KTPH018GooseKTPH019 — is running inside one of your KTPH020local shell tabsKTPH021 and keeps track of what it is currently doing: working, waiting for your answer, finished, or sitting idle at its prompt. The analysis happens entirely inside korTTY on your own machine. What it finds is shown wherever you look: as a glyph in the tab title, as chips and accents in the dashboard, in a dockable KTPH022Coding AgentsKTPH023 panel with quick answers and a prompt box, as a strip in the status bar, as a count on the app icon and, when you are not looking at the pane, as a desktop notification. This page explains what is detected, how each of these surfaces works, how to switch things off, and how to adjust or extend the screen rules when an agent changes its user interface.

Detection covers the ten agents below, started from a KTPH005Local ShellKTPH006 tab — directly, through a package-manager wrapper such as KTPH000, or as a KTPH001, KTPH002, KTPH003 or KTPH004 script. SSH and Mosh tabs are not analysed, because the agent runs on the remote machine and korTTY cannot see its process; an agent on a server can still tell you that it waits for you with a terminal notification, see KTPH007Notifications from programsKTPH008.
KTPH000 (the running agent renames its process to KTPH001; korTTY reads that process title when KTPH002 reports no script)
KTPH000, KTPH001 (the launcher starts a bundled KTPH002 on KTPH003; korTTY recognises that install path)
KTPH000 (a Python console script, also KTPH001)
KTPH000 (its screen rules are not yet verified against live sessions; Amp shows up from its first working or approval screen)
KTPH000 (Block's goose CLI; the database-migration tool of the same name is never reported)

Every split pane is tracked on its own, so a tab with two panes can show one agent working while the other waits for a permission decision. A pane that runs no agent, or whose agent has exited, simply has no detection result.
A detected agent is always in exactly one of five states. The list is ordered by urgency: when several panes are summarised, the most urgent state wins.
The agent is waiting for you — a permission dialog (KTPH001Do you want to proceed?KTPH002), a question picker, or a KTPH000 prompt is on screen.

The agent has finished. Either it shows an explicit completion screen that a rule recognises, or — far more often — it went from WORKING back to its empty prompt while you were not looking at its pane. KorTTY then keeps it marked DONE (✓) until you look at the pane; the moment its tab is selected and its pane focused in the front window, it becomes IDLE.
The agent is thinking, running a tool or streaming output — typically recognisable by its spinner line and the KTPH000esc to interruptKTPH001 hint.
The agent is running and its input box is empty, waiting for your next instruction.
The agent process is present but the screen matches none of the rules and the rule file asks for a strict result instead of a fallback.

KTPH004
Open the KTPH005dashboardKTPH006 with KTPH007View → Show DashboardKTPH008 (KTPH009KTPH001KTPH010+KTPH011KTPH002KTPH012+KTPH013KTPH003KTPH014) and every connection row that hosts a coding agent shows a KTPH015chipKTPH016 after the protocol badge: the state glyph, the agent's short name (or the alias you gave it) and, for an agent that is waiting, working or done, how long it has been in that state (KTPH000). An idle agent gets a dim, outlined chip so you still see that one is present. A row that also runs korTTY's own AI agent merges both marks into one chip.

The row itself carries a coloured KTPH002accent barKTPH003 on its left edge — amber while the agent waits for you (the row is tinted as well), blue while it works, green when it is done — and the status dot of a waiting agent pulses while the window is in front and animations are enabled. Group and environment rows above a marked connection show a KTPH004rollup chipKTPH005 such as KTPH000 and take the accent of their most urgent child, and the footer appends the same rollup to the connection count (KTPH001), so a waiting agent is visible even when its group is collapsed.

A split tab grows KTPH002pane rowsKTPH003 below the connection (KTPH000, named after the pane's working directory, with your home directory written KTPH001 as the shell writes it), one per pane, so each pane can be reached on its own. Every pane is listed, whether or not an agent was detected in it: a split where one pane runs an agent and the other does not is the ordinary case, and showing only the agent's pane would hide half the tab. A pane without an agent carries no chip and no accent. An unsplit tab gets no pane rows, because its connection row already is the pane. When an agent becomes blocked, the dashboard KTPH004expandsKTPH005 the tree down to its row once per transition — a waiting agent is never hidden inside a collapsed group — and respects KTPH006Collapse allKTPH007 afterwards.

The context menu of a marked row adds KTPH000Focus PaneKTPH001, which selects the tab and focuses exactly that pane, KTPH002Show in Coding Agents PanelKTPH003, which docks the panel and selects the agent, and, while the agent waits for you, KTPH004Send EnterKTPH005, KTPH006Send EscKTPH007 and KTPH008Interrupt (Ctrl+C)KTPH009 to answer the dialog without leaving the dashboard. The tab title shows the same glyph as the chip — ✋ waiting, ⚡ working, ✓ done, merged with korTTY's own AI-agent glyph where both apply.

KTPH003
The panel lists every detected agent of every korTTY window in one place. Open it with KTPH004View → Coding Agents → Dock Left / Dock RightKTPH005, toggle it on its last-used side with KTPH006Show/HideKTPH007 (KTPH008KTPH000KTPH009+KTPH010KTPH001KTPH011+KTPH012KTPH002KTPH013), from the ⋯ menu inside the panel, from the status strip's context menu, or with KTPH014Show in Coding Agents PanelKTPH015 in the dashboard. Placement and width are remembered across restarts. Agents that wait for you are listed first (longest waiting on top), then the working, done and idle ones in window, tab and pane order; the row of the pane you are currently in carries a left accent.

Every row shows the state dot and name, a state chip such as KTPH000, the location line (KTPH001) and the last screen line that matched a rule — the evidence. Below them sit the KTPH002quick keysKTPH003: KTPH004FocusKTPH005 brings the pane to the front, KTPH006yKTPH007, KTPH008nKTPH009, KTPH010EnterKTPH011 and KTPH012EscKTPH013 answer a dialog (they are highlighted while the agent waits for you), KTPH014↑KTPH015 and KTPH016↓KTPH017 move through a question picker, KTPH018Ctrl+CKTPH019 interrupts, KTPH020ExplainKTPH021 opens a drawer with the full detection explanation (agent, state, matching rule, evidence, process and time in state), and KTPH022Rename…KTPH023 gives the agent an alias that replaces its name in every chip, row and notification — an empty alias restores the agent name, and the alias survives a reconnect but is dropped when the pane closes. Every key goes to the pane's own terminal connection, exactly as if you had typed it there; the buttons are disabled while the pane is not connected.

The KTPH006prompt boxKTPH007 at the bottom sends longer text to the agent selected in the target list: KTPH008KTPH003KTPH009 sends, KTPH010KTPH004KTPH011+KTPH012KTPH005KTPH013 inserts a line break. A single line is sent followed by Enter. A multi-line prompt is wrapped in bracketed paste — so the agent receives it as one pasted block instead of several submitted lines — but only when that agent has switched bracketed paste on, which Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, MiniMax Code, Qwen Code, OpenCode, Cursor Agent, Aider and Goose all do at their prompt; otherwise the lines are sent as typed. Bracketed-paste markers inside the prompt text itself (KTPH000, KTPH001 and their 8-bit forms) are removed before sending, so a prompt can never end the paste early and have its remaining lines submitted one by one. Two prompts are refused with a message in the panel's status line instead of being sent: while the agent is KTPH014waiting for a decisionKTPH015 the KTPH016SendKTPH017 button stays disabled, because the text would land inside the permission dialog — answer it with y, n, Enter or Esc first; and a prompt whose first line starts with KTPH018korTTY's own AI shortcutKTPH019 (the command name configured under Settings → AI, KTPH002 by default) is rejected, because korTTY's shortcut filter would divert that line to its own AI agent instead of the coding agent — rephrase the line. Errors of a quick key or prompt (pane closed, not connected, write failed) appear in the same status line for a few seconds, never as a dialog, and a successful send confirms with KTPH020Sent to Claude CodeKTPH021.

The KTPH003Next blockedKTPH004 button in the panel header jumps to the next agent that waits for you, across all windows and wrapping around; it is the same action as KTPH005KTPH000KTPH006+KTPH007KTPH001KTPH008+KTPH009KTPH002KTPH010 and a click on the status strip.

KTPH001
The right end of the status bar shows a compact strip while at least one coding agent is known: up to three chips for waiting, working and done agents (KTPH000, zero counts are omitted), with the waiting dot pulsing while the window is in front. A click jumps to the next agent waiting for you — or, when none is waiting, to the first agent in display order — and a right-click offers KTPH002Show/HideKTPH003 for the panel and KTPH004Next Blocked AgentKTPH005. The tooltip summarises the counts. The strip disappears together with the status bar when you hide it under KTPH006ViewKTPH007.

KTPH003
The number of agents waiting for a decision — across all windows — is shown as a KTPH004badge on the app iconKTPH005 so you notice it while working in another application. How the badge is drawn depends on the platform: on KTPH006macOSKTPH007 the packaged app sets the Dock badge; on KTPH008WindowsKTPH009 korTTY draws the count into its own taskbar and title-bar icon; on KTPH010LinuxKTPH011 it emits the launcher-entry signal that KDE Plasma, Ubuntu Dock and Dash to Dock render on the launcher icon — this needs an installed desktop file (the deb, rpm or pacman package) and a reachable session bus, which korTTY talks to directly. Stock GNOME Shell without a dock extension shows no launcher counters at all. Wherever no icon badge is available — an unpacked archive, KTPH000, an unsupported desktop — korTTY falls back to the KTPH012window titleKTPH013, which becomes KTPH001 while two agents wait and returns to KTPH002 at zero. When an agent becomes blocked while no korTTY window is focused, the app additionally asks for attention once (the Dock icon bounces, the launcher entry is marked urgent).

A KTPH001desktop notificationKTPH002 is shown when an agent needs a decision or finishes while you are not looking at its pane — that is, while its tab is not the selected tab of the front window, or its pane is not the focused one. The title names the agent (KTPH003Claude Code needs a decisionKTPH004, KTPH005Claude Code finishedKTPH006), the body shows the location and working directory followed by the matching screen line. A blocked state has to persist for a moment before it is reported, an agent is reported at most once every ten seconds, the same transition is never reported twice, and nothing is shown for the pane you are looking at. Notifications use the operating system's own service: the Notification Center on KTPH007macOSKTPH008, the tray balloon on KTPH009WindowsKTPH010, and KTPH000 on KTPH011LinuxKTPH012 (through the host in the Flatpak package). Nothing leaves this computer — the text is the screen line korTTY already read.

Both surfaces are on by default and have their own toggles under KTPH000Settings → Terminal → Coding agentsKTPH001 (see KTPH002Enabling detectionKTPH003). Switching the badge off clears it immediately; switching notifications off stops new ones without touching the badge.
Show or hide the Coding Agents panel on its last-used side (right by default)
Jump to the next coding agent waiting for a decision, across windows
In the panel's prompt box: send the prompt / insert a line break
On macOS use KTPH002KTPH000KTPH003 where KTPH004KTPH001KTPH005 is shown.

KorTTY only believes an agent is present when two independent observations agree — this KTPH001double evidenceKTPH002 keeps a stray KTPH000 in a shell script or a quoted prompt fragment from producing false alarms:

KTPH003Process tree.KTPH004 The pane's local shell has a known process ID. KorTTY walks that process's descendants and looks for the newest live one whose executable name — or, for KTPH000, KTPH001 and KTPH002, the script it runs — belongs to one of the supported agents.

KTPH000Screen rules.KTPH001 The text currently visible in the pane (never the scrollback), together with the window title the agent sets and whether it switched to the alternate screen, is matched against the rule file of that agent. The first rule match confirms the process; from then on the rules decide the state.

The screen is re-evaluated about 200 ms after the first change in a burst of output — further changes inside that window are coalesced — so a long stream of output triggers one evaluation per 200 ms window instead of one per line, and a short burst exactly one. A slow heartbeat additionally notices when the agent exits without printing anything, when the tab disconnects, or when you switch detection off. Rules are evaluated by priority; the first rule whose conditions all hold determines the state. If the agent process is confirmed but no rule matches, the rule file's fallback state (IDLE for the bundled files) is reported.

Screen text is analysed only inside korTTY, in memory, on this computer. Nothing is sent to any service, written to disk, or handed to the AI assistant — detection is plain pattern matching against local rule files. If you prefer not to have local shell screens inspected at all, switch the feature off under KTPH000Settings → Terminal → Coding agentsKTPH001.

Detection is on by default and is controlled by three toggles in KTPH000Settings → TerminalKTPH001, section KTPH002Coding agentsKTPH003. Changing them takes effect immediately for all open tabs — no restart or reconnect is needed.
Detect coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, MiniMax Code, Qwen Code, OpenCode, Cursor Agent, Aider, Amp, Goose) in local shell tabs
Desktop notification when a coding agent needs a decision or finishes while you are not looking at its pane
Show the number of agents waiting for a decision on the app icon

When the detection toggle is off, korTTY neither walks the process tree nor reads the screen of any pane, and the dashboard marks, panel, strip, badge and notifications all fall silent. The panel's placement and width are not settings-dialog options: they follow the KTPH005View → Coding AgentsKTPH006 menu and are stored as KTPH000 (KTPH001, KTPH002 or KTPH003) and KTPH004.
Each agent's screen rules live in a small JSON file. KorTTY ships one bundled file per agent and lets you replace it with your own copy under your configuration directory:

An override replaces the bundled file for that agent KTPH001as a wholeKTPH002 — there is no merging, so start from the bundled file and edit it. The file must be a regular file (symbolic links are not followed), and its KTPH000 must match the file name. An invalid file — malformed JSON, an unknown key, a bad regular expression, a duplicate rule id, or a rule without any condition — is ignored with a warning in the log and the bundled rules stay in effect, so a typo can never silently disable detection. Rule files are read at startup; restart korTTY after editing one.
The schema is strict: every key not listed here is an error, so misspelt keys are reported instead of being ignored.
The agent this file describes; must match the file name (KTPH000, KTPH001, KTPH002, KTPH003, KTPH004, KTPH005, KTPH006, KTPH007, KTPH008, KTPH009).
Free text for your own notes, for example which agent version the rules were verified against.
State reported while the agent process is present but no rule matches. Defaults to KTPH000; KTPH001 makes detection stricter.
The list of rules, evaluated by descending KTPH000; ties keep file order. May be empty.
Unique within the file; letters, digits, KTPH000, KTPH001 and KTPH002. Shown in diagnostics so you can see which rule fired.
The state this rule reports: KTPH000, KTPH001, KTPH002 or KTPH003.
KTPH000 restricts matching to the bottom N non-empty screen lines; KTPH001 or absent means the whole screen.
Regular expressions tried against each line of the region; the first matching line becomes the rule's evidence.

Agents change their interfaces often, and a rule that matched last month may silently stop matching after an update. KorTTY's bundled rules are therefore pinned by KTPH000screen fixturesKTPH001: for every agent, the repository keeps captured terminal screens with the state and rule they must produce, and the test suite fails as soon as a bundled rule no longer matches its fixture or a rule has no fixture at all. When you notice a wrong or missing state, the most useful report is the visible screen text of the pane at that moment, the agent and its version, and the state you expected — it becomes a new fixture and a rule fix in the next release. Until then, a local override file lets you correct the rule for yourself immediately.

The repository ships a recorder for exactly this purpose: KTPH000 runs an agent inside a pseudo-terminal and passes your keyboard through, so the session behaves like a normal terminal. From then on the test suite guards the rule against that screen, and a rule change that would break it is caught before release.
